{{Short description|Notion from Computability}}

In [[computable analysis]], '''Weihrauch reducibility''' is a notion of reducibility between [[multi-valued function]]s on represented spaces that roughly captures the uniform computational strength of [[computational problem]]s.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last1=Brattka |first1=Vasco |chapter=Weihrauch Complexity in Computable Analysis |date=2021 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-030-59234-9_11 |title=Handbook of Computability and Complexity in Analysis |pages=367–417 |editor-last=Brattka |editor-first=Vasco |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-59234-9_11 |isbn=978-3-030-59233-2 |access-date=2022-06-29 |last2=Gherardi |first2=Guido |last3=Pauly |first3=Arno |s2cid=7903709 |editor2-last=Hertling |editor2-first=Peter|arxiv=1707.03202 }}</ref> It was originally introduced by {{ill|Klaus Weihrauch|de}} in an unpublished 1992 technical report.<ref>{{cite report | last=Weihrauch | first=Klaus | title=The Degrees of Discontinuity of some Translators between Representations of the Real Numbers | series=Informatik-Berichte | volume=129 | publisher=FernUniversität in Hagen | date=1992 | url=https://nbn-resolving.org/urn:nbn:de:hbz:708-dh6698}}</ref>

== Definition ==

A ''represented space'' is a pair <math display="inline">(X,\delta)</math> of a set <math>X</math>  and a [[surjective]] [[partial function]] <math>\delta:\subset \mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}\rightarrow X</math>.<ref name=":0" />

Let <math>(X,\delta_X)</math> and <math>(Y,\delta_Y)</math> be represented spaces and let <math> f:\subset X \rightrightarrows Y </math> be a partial multi-valued function. A ''realizer'' for <math>f</math> is a (possibly partial) function <math>F:\subset \mathbb{N}^\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}^\mathbb{N}</math> such that, for every <math>p \in \mathrm{dom} f \circ \delta_X</math>, <math> \delta_Y \circ F (p) = f\circ \delta_X(p)</math>. Intuitively, a realizer <math>F</math> for <math>f</math> behaves "just like <math>f</math>" but it works on names. If <math>F</math> is a realizer for <math>f</math> we write <math> F \vdash f</math>.

Let <math>X,Y,Z,W</math> be represented spaces and let <math> f:\subset X \rightrightarrows Y, g:\subset Z \rightrightarrows W</math> be partial multi-valued functions. We say that <math>f</math> is ''Weihrauch reducible'' to <math>g</math>, and write <math>f\le_{\mathrm{W}} g</math>, if there are [[computable]] partial functions <math>\Phi,\Psi:\subset \mathbb{N}^\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}^\mathbb{N}</math> such that<math display="block"> (\forall G \vdash g )( \Psi \langle \mathrm{id}, G\Phi \rangle \vdash f ),</math>where <math>\Psi \langle \mathrm{id}, G\Phi \rangle:= \langle p,q\rangle \mapsto \Psi(\langle p, G\Phi(q) \rangle) </math> and <math> \langle \cdot \rangle</math> denotes the join in the [[Baire space (set theory)|Baire space]]. Very often, in the literature we find <math> \Psi </math> written as a binary function, so to avoid the use of the join.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022}} In other words, <math>f \le_\mathrm{W} g</math> if there are two computable maps <math>\Phi, \Psi</math> such that the function <math>p \mapsto \Psi(p, q) </math> is a realizer for <math>f</math> whenever <math>q</math> is a solution for <math>g(\Phi(p))</math>. The maps <math>\Phi, \Psi</math> are often called ''forward'' and ''backward'' functional respectively.

We say that <math>f</math> is ''strongly Weihrauch reducible'' to <math>g</math>, and write <math> f\le_{\mathrm{sW}} g</math>, if the backward functional <math>\Psi</math> does not have access to the original input. In symbols:<math display="block"> (\forall G \vdash g )( \Psi G\Phi \vdash f ).</math>
